findings.title: Able2Shell: Frequently asked questions for reported N-able N-central zero-day vulnerabilities
findings.summary: N-able released a hotfix for N-central that fixes seven CVEs after a researcher published proof-of-concept code for 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities. The researcher says one attack chain needs no credentials. Key Takeaways Able2Shell is a set of 33 alleged vulnerabilities in N-able N-central, published with proof-of-concept code. The researcher says one chain lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands on the server. Security firms report exploitation attempts against N-central honeypots, but as of November 10, no confirmed compromise of a customer server has been reported. N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 on November 10. It fixes seven CVEs. Background Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Able2Shell, a set of reported zero-day vulnerabilities in N-able N-central. FAQ When was Able2Shell first disclosed? A researcher operating under the GitHub account “Oracle-Security” published a write-up titled “Able2Shell” in the account’s CVEs repository. It describes 33 alleged N-central vulnerabilities with proof-of-concept code. The earliest README commit is dated November 9, 2026 at 04:14 UTC. N-able described the release as a public disclosure by an independent security researcher. N-able does not state whether it was notified in advance and does not name the researcher. What are the vulnerabilities associated with Able2Shell? On November 10, N-able published seven CVE records for vulnerabilities fixed in N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2. On its status page, N-able says the release addresses “the most critical November 9 vulnerabilities” and that a follow-up hotfix will provide further security updates. The page lists all seven as related CVEs. One, CVE-2026-91000 , had been reserved on September 14, before the public Able2Shell disclosure. findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. New attack discovery By proactively discovering and cataloging new attack vectors through internal and external programs, we can identify vulnerabilities and deploy robust defenses ahead of adversarial activity. Human Red-Teaming Human Red-Teaming uses adversarial simulations to uncover security and safety vulnerabilities. Specialized teams execute attacks based on realistic user profiles to exploit weaknesses, coordinating with product teams to resolve identified issues. Automated Red-Teaming Automated Red-Teaming is done via dynamic, machine-learning-driven frameworks to stress-test environments. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. findings.title: Rust in Android: move fast and fix things
findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. In this post, we dig into the data behind this shift and also cover: How we’re expanding our reach: We're pushing to make secure code the default across our entire software stack. We have updates on Rust adoption in first-party apps, the Linux kernel, and firmware. Our first rust memory safety vulnerability...almost: We'll analyze a near-miss memory safety bug in unsafe Rust: how it happened, how it was mitigated, and steps we're taking to prevent recurrence. It’s also a good chance to answer the question “if Rust can have memory safety issues, why bother at all?” Building Better Software, Faster Developing an operating system requires the low-level control and predictability of systems programming languages like C, C++, and Rust. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.title: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite
findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: AG2: Newline injection in SandboxShellTool bypasses allowed=[...] and readonly=True, enabling arbitrary command execution
findings.summary:
### Summary
SandboxShellTool's restricted modes — allowed=[...] (explicit command allowlist) and readonly=True (implicit READONLY_COMMANDS allowlist) — can both be bypassed by embedding a newline character inside the command string. The filter only inspects a single-line set of shell metacharacters, but execution runs the raw string through `sh -c`, where a shell treats an embedded newline exactly like a `;` statement separator. An agent (or content that steers the agent, e.g. via prompt injection) can therefore run arbitrary shell commands even when the tool was configured to allow only a specific command prefix or only read-only commands. With the default LocalEnvironment() backend this is a real host subprocess (its own docstring: "Commands run via subprocess on the host, so there is no real isolation"), not an isolated container, so this is full host command execution, not merely an escape from an already-sandboxed environment.

### Details
Both restricted modes are enforced by `ShellAdapter._filter()` in `ag2/tools/sandbox/adapter/shell.py`:

```python
def _filter(self, command: str) -> str | None:
    if self._allowed is not None:
        if not any(matches(p, command) for p in self._allowed):
            return f"Command not allowed: {command!r}"
        if contains_shell_operator(command):
            return f"Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): {command!r}"
    ...
```

`readonly=True` reuses this exact same branch: `SandboxShellTool.__init__` / `ShellAdapter.__init__` sets `self._allowed = list(READONLY_COMMANDS)` when `readonly` is set and no explicit `allowed` is given, so both modes share one filter and one bypass.

`contains_shell_operator()` in `ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py` checks the command against:

```python
_SHELL_OPERATORS: tuple[str, ...] = (">", ">>", "|", ";", "&&", "||", "`", "$(")
```

This tuple has no entry for `\n` (or `\r`). `matches()` only checks that the command starts with an allowed prefix fo

findings.summary: Advisory at a Glance Title Chinese Government-linked Cyber Threat Actors Combine Automated and Hands-on Hacking Tools to Steal Sensitive Data Original Publication October 8, 2026 Executive Summary Chinese government-linked cyber threat actors, enabled by the Integrity Technology Group, are combining automated scanning tools, large-scale botnets, and hands-on exploitation techniques to target and steal sensitive data from organizations worldwide, including US critical infrastructure sectors. These actors exploit vulnerabilities by using scanning tools, cross-site scripting attacks, and password spraying on Microsoft Exchange servers, while establishing persistence through VPN software and exfiltrating emails and credentials using scripts. To help mitigate against this activity, organizations should prioritize disabling unused services and ports, sanitizing web application inputs to prevent injection attacks, implementing multifactor authentication for all services, and applying timely patches to reduce risks of compromise. findings.title: #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware
findings.summary: Advisory at a Glance Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware Original Publication October 20, 2026 Executive Summary This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Next, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks. findings.title: React: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in React Server Components
findings.summary:
### Impact

Crafted payloads targeting frameworks supporting React Server Components can lead to remote code execution. This only affects extremely rare cases where responses transport multiple typed arrays and an attacker-controlled value.

Updating immediately is recommended.

The vulnerability exists in versions 19.0.0 through 19.0.8, 19.1.0 through 19.1.9, 19.2.0 through 19.2.8 and 19.3.0 of:

- react-server-dom-webpack
- react-server-dom-parcel
- react-server-dom-turbopack

### Patches

Fixes were back ported to versions 19.0.09, 19.1.10, 19.2.9, and 19.3.1.

If applications are using any of the above packages please upgrade to any of the fixed versions immediately.

If an app’s React code does not use a server, the app is not affected by this vulnerability. If an app does not use a framework, bundler, or bundler plugin that supports React Server Components, the app is not affected by this vulnerability.

findings.title: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file read and remote code execution in video previews, analysis and image processing
findings.summary:
### Impact
`ActiveStorage::Blob#open` writes a blob to a tempfile whose name carries the extension of the uploaded filename, and hands that path to `ffprobe` (`VideoAnalyzer`, `AudioAnalyzer`), `ffmpeg` (`VideoPreviewer`) and ImageMagick (`ImageAnalyzer`, the `:mini_magick` variant processor). These tools select a decoder from the file extension when the content does not identify its own format, so an attacker who chooses the filename and declares the content type of an upload chooses which decoder processes it. An FFmpeg built with AviSynth support treats a file with the `.avs` extension as an AviSynth script and evaluates it, which could disclose files readable by the application process through the preview image, or load a native library the attacker has also uploaded, possibly leading to remote code execution in the FFmpeg process. ImageMagick selects its coders and delegates from the extension in the same way.

### Details
The fixed releases keep the uploaded extension on the tempfile only when Marcel maps that extension to the blob's recorded content type, and name the tempfile with no extension otherwise. A form upload whose Rack tempfile fails the same check is copied to a correctly named tempfile before processing. Files whose uploaded extension disagrees with their content type are still processed; the external tool detects their format from the content. The Active Storage CHANGELOG describes the change.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Accepts uploads from untrusted users.
- Analyzes video or audio attachments (which Active Storage does on attach by default), generates video previews, or processes images with ImageMagick.

The AviSynth attack additionally requires an FFmpeg built with `--enable-avisynth` and the AviSynthPlus runtime on the host. Upstream FFmpeg and the common Linux distribution and Homebrew packages do not enable it; the GPL builds distributed for Windows and Linux from ffmpeg.

findings.title: Action Pack: Possible restoration of destroyed sessions in Action Dispatch CacheStore
findings.summary:
### Impact
`ActionDispatch::Session::CacheStore` writes a session back to the cache at the end of each request that loaded it, without checking that the session's cache entry still exists. When a concurrent request destroys the session, through `reset_session` on logout or by deleting its cache entry on the server, a request that loaded the session earlier and finishes later restores it under its original session ID. Logout and server-side revocation could therefore fail to end a session, and an attacker who holds a stolen session cookie could keep that session valid across the victim's logout.

Applications that use `config.session_store :cache_store` are affected, with any cache backend. `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` is not affected, nor is `ActionDispatch::Session::MemCacheStore` with Dalli 4.0.0 or later, whose session store does not write back a session that was deleted.

### Details
The fixed releases record which session a request loaded and skip the write when that session's cache entry no longer exists. Changes that such a request makes to the destroyed session are discarded, and Rack logs a warning that the session could not be saved. Each request that writes back a session it loaded makes one additional cache read.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/d479192cf88a8b30a335a8bc25188a2d8e0f8d9f.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/5bb5ec66ed8faaf590ffe1222d7a5eb6e9d050f5.patch

### Credit
Found by the team during internal code review.

findings.title: JRuby: NONET is bypassed for external DTDs and entities when the systemId uses a short-form IPv4 host
findings.summary:
### Summary

On JRuby, the `NONET` parse option did not block an external DTD or entity whose system identifier used a short-form IPv4 host, such as `http://127.1/` or `http://169.254.43518/`, or was an absolute path such as `/x.dtd` in a document parsed from a network URL. An application that parses untrusted XML with `DTDLOAD`, `DTDVALID` or `NOENT` could be made to send network requests, potentially enabling SSRF.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 applies the `XML::Schema` check from [GHSA-8678-w3jw-xfc2](https://github.com/sparklemotion/nokogiri/security/advisories/GHSA-8678-w3jw-xfc2): with `NONET` set, only local resources are loaded.

Only JRuby is affected. Default parse options are not affected.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later, or do not enable `DTDLOAD`, `DTDVALID` or `NOENT` for untrusted input.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by @arpitjain099.

findings.title: Rack: Multipart boundary ambiguity guard in Rack::Multipart::Parser can be bypassed with a quoted boundary value, allowing WAF bypass
findings.summary:
## Summary

The guard added for CVE-2026-26961 (GHSA-vgpv-f759-9wx3), which rejects multipart requests with more than one `boundary` parameter, only inspects the part of the `Content-Type` header after the boundary it extracts. A `Content-Type` whose first `boundary` parameter is empty or begins with a quote, semicolon, or comma is skipped by the extraction pattern, so a second `boundary` parameter is accepted silently and Rack parses the body with a boundary that a conforming parser would not derive from the header.

## Details

`Rack::Multipart::Parser.parse_boundary` extracts the boundary with a regular expression that uses a lazy prefix and a value class excluding `"`, `;`, and `,`. For a header such as `multipart/form-data; boundary=";boundary=AaB03x"` or `multipart/form-data; boundary=; boundary=AaB03x`, the pattern skips the first `boundary=` and anchors on the second, and the subsequent check for another `boundary=` in the remaining text finds nothing. Rack then uses `AaB03x`.

RFC 9110 parses the first header as a single parameter whose value is `;boundary=AaB03x`, which is not a legal boundary under RFC 2046, so the only conformant outcome is rejection. Inspecting intermediaries that implement the standard grammar, such as ModSecurity, see a different boundary or no multipart body at all.

The fix counts `boundary=` occurrences across the entire header value and rejects the request when there is more than one.

## Impact

As with CVE-2026-26961, an attacker can craft a multipart request that a web application firewall or other inspecting proxy in front of a Rack application interprets differently from Rack, so form fields and file uploads reach the application without inspection. Rack itself grants no capability beyond that of a well-formed request with the same body. All supported versions, including 2.2, are affected.

## Mitigation

* Update to a patched version of Rack.
* Reject requests whose `Content-Type` contains more than one `boundary` parameter

findings.title: NocoBase: @nocobase/plugin-action-custom-request allows server-side request forgery through runtime URL overrides
findings.summary:
### Summary

A Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability exists in NocoBase v2.1.10 in the `@nocobase/plugin-action-custom-request` plugin.

A low-privileged authenticated user can call the `customRequests:send` endpoint and override the stored request URL at runtime using `options.url`. This causes the NocoBase server to perform outbound HTTP requests to attacker-controlled or internal URLs.

* Product: NocoBase
* Version: v2.1.10
* Component: `@nocobase/plugin-action-custom-request`
* Severity: Moderate
* Required privilege: authenticated low-privileged user / member

Testing was performed only in a local Docker lab environment at `http://127.0.0.1:13000`. No public NocoBase instance was tested.

Lab environment:

* Docker image: `nocobase/nocobase:latest-full`
* Commit: `23e2bd35625439594e4757bac31d57c9e8e695b9`
* Database: PostgreSQL 16
* Containers: `nocobase-lab`, `nocobase-postgres`
* Docker network: `172.19.0.0/16`
* Important environment variable: `SERVER_REQUEST_WHITELIST` was not set

---

### Details

The vulnerable endpoint is:

```http
POST /api/customRequests:send?filterByTk=<key>
```

The `customRequests:send` action is allowed for any logged-in user:

```ts
// plugin-action-custom-request/src/server/plugin.ts
this.app.acl.allow('customRequests', ['send', 'listByCurrentRole'], 'loggedIn');
```

The request options supplied at runtime are merged into the stored request configuration. This allows a low-privileged user to override the stored URL:

```ts

  ...(requestConfig.options || {}),
  ...omitNullAndUndefined(runtimeOptions || {}),
};

const { url, ...options } = mergedOptions;
```

The URL is therefore attacker-controlled when the low-privileged user sends a request body such as:

```json
{
  "options": {
    "url": "http://attacker-controlled-host:18080/ssrf-proof",
    "method": "GET"
  }
}
```

findings.title: compose-lint: Text in a pull request can still issue CI workflow commands through compose-lint 0.31.0's output
findings.summary:
### Impact

0.31.0 fixed GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, where text from a Compose file became GitHub Actions workflow commands in compose-lint's output. The fix escapes the command openers in everything compose-lint prints, and the 0.31.0 changelog says the report "escapes both openers (also covering Azure Pipelines)". Five paths were left open:

- **Unicode whitespace before a line-leading `::`.** The runner strips all Unicode whitespace from the start of a line before it looks for a command. compose-lint only accounted for spaces and tabs, so a no-break space or another Unicode space ahead of `::` is not escaped. It can come from a Compose value, or from a file name: the text report's file heading and per-file summary, and the `fix` summary on stderr, start with the path as given, so a directory named with a leading no-break space followed by `::` puts a command at the start of a line. This reaches those lines, the text report's fix guidance, the `fix` dry-run diff, and continuation lines of stderr diagnostics.
- **JSON and SARIF printed to stdout.** `--format json` and `--format sarif` output never passed through the sanitizer, so `##[` inside a service name or other value reaches the log intact when the output isn't redirected to a file.
- **Command-line errors.** When a repository path reaches compose-lint's arguments without a `--` before it, the argument parser prints it raw in its error message. That includes a carriage return, which the runner treats as a line break, so a command can also start a new line there.
- **Azure Pipelines.** `##vso[` logging commands were not escaped on any path, despite the changelog's Azure claim.
- **An error message in the GitHub Action (0.30.0 and 0.31.0).** When `sarif-file:` names a file in a subdirectory that can't be created, the Action prints the directory's resolved path in an error message, outside the window in which it turns command processing off. A pull request can commit a symlink on that path to a directory whose name cont

findings.title: Forge: Incomplete PKCS#7 padding validation in AES/DES CBC and ECB decryption
findings.summary:
### Summary
`decipher.finish()` in CBC and ECB mode accepted malformed PKCS#7 padding: only the last byte was checked, against a limit of four blocks, so mismatched padding bytes, a zero count and oversized counts were accepted and up to four blocks of plaintext could be silently removed. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`modes.cbc.prototype.unpad()` and `modes.ecb.prototype.unpad()` in `lib/cipherModes.js` read the last decrypted byte as the PKCS#7 padding count, rejected it only if it was larger than `blockSize << 2` (64 for AES, 32 for DES), and then removed that many bytes. They did not reject a count of 0 or a count larger than one block, and did not check that every padding byte equals the count, as PKCS#7 (RFC 5652 section 6.3) requires. On the Wycheproof AES-CBC-PKCS5 test vectors, 69 of 144 invalid vectors decrypted successfully.

CBC and ECB without a MAC do not provide integrity: an attacker who can modify ciphertext can already make the final block decrypt to any padding. The effect of this bug is that malformed ciphertext is accepted as valid and that oversized counts silently truncate up to four blocks of plaintext. The fix does not protect against padding oracle attacks; applications that decrypt untrusted CBC data need to authenticate it (for example with an HMAC) or use AES-GCM.

The fix requires a count from 1 to the block size and checks every padding byte. Data with other padding schemes that only use the last byte as the count (ANSI X.923, ISO 10126, XML Encryption) now fails to decrypt with default unpadding; set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` before `finish()` and remove such padding in application code.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. CBC and ECB decryption requires valid PKCS#7 padding.

#### Workarounds
Authenticate CBC/ECB ciphertext before decrypting it, or use AES-GCM. To check padding on 1.4.0, set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` and validate the padding in application code.

#### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc

findings.title: Forge: ASN.1 resource exhaustion via BIT STRING decoding in asn1.fromDer
findings.summary:
### Summary
`asn1.fromDer()` decodes the contents of BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 by default. That decode ignored the `maxDepth` recursion limit (an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031) and also decoded nested BIT STRINGs, keeping a full copy of the decoded contents at each level, so small crafted DER or PEM inputs (certificates, keys, PKCS structures) use excessive CPU time and memory and can abort the Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`asn1.fromDer()` attempts by default to decode the contents of primitive BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 (`decodeBitStrings`, default `true`). Two flaws in that decode in `lib/asn1.js` allow resource exhaustion:

1. `_fromDer()` started the BIT STRING decode with a new options object, `{strict: true, decodeBitStrings: true}`, that did not include `maxDepth`. Inside that decode the depth check compared against `undefined` and never triggered, so the recursion limit added for CVE-2025-66031 (GHSA-554w-wpv2-vw27) was not enforced for anything below a decoded BIT STRING. Both the global `asn1.maxDepth` (default 256) and the per-call `maxDepth` option were ignored there. Errors in this speculative decode, including stack overflows, are caught and the contents kept as raw bytes, so deep nesting is parsed instead of rejected. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031.
2. BIT STRINGs nested inside decoded BIT STRING contents were decoded as well, and `asn1.create()` gives each decoded BIT STRING a deep copy of its decoded contents (`obj.original`, used by `toDer()` to detect changes). Memory use therefore grows quadratically with the nesting depth, even within the default depth limit.

No specification is violated; the parser lacks a resource limit.

The fix passes `maxDepth` to the BIT STRING decode, and decodes BIT STRING contents with `decodeBitStrings: false`, so only one level of BIT STRING contents is decoded. Contents that would exceed the limit, and BIT STRINGs inside decoded BIT STRING contents, are kept as undecoded BIT STRING v

findings.title: compose-lint: Incomplete fix for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg: a run stopped at the finding limit quotes a secret from a CI-generated `.env`
findings.summary:
### Impact

This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg. 0.32.0 made findings quote the `${NAME}` a sibling `.env` filled in, instead of its value. The same release added a stop at 20,000 findings per document, and that stop is checked before the quoting step. A run that hits it reports the findings graded so far with the resolved values still in them, in text, JSON and SARIF output. That happens with or without `--allow-partial-coverage`.

The attack is the one GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg describes. In a CI workflow that writes secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file, a pull request changes a line to `image: "${DB_PASSWORD}"`. It also pushes the document past 20,000 findings, which a few hundred lines can do, because an aliased list is graded once for each service that uses it. The secret's value is quoted in a finding that reaches the job log, the JSON output and the SARIF uploaded to Code Scanning. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text. The run exits 2, or 0 with `--allow-partial-coverage`, after the output has been written.

The preconditions are the same as for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg. The workflow writes secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file *and* runs on pull requests from authors who should not see them, such as a `pull_request_target` workflow that lints the pull request's files. Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, so the common setup is not exposed. The inflated document is visible in the pull request, but the workflow runs before anyone reviews it.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**Python package.** `compose-lint` 0.32.0. Earlier releases have no finding limit, and their quoting gap is GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg itself.

**GitHub Action.** Action tag v0.32.0 is affected. Tags before v0.22.0 install the newest release unless `version:` is set, so they currently install 0.32.0.

**pre-commit hook.** `rev: v0.32.0`.

findings.title: GPUStack: Missing authorization on several cluster and resource endpoints allows cross-user access and cluster takeover
findings.summary:
### Impact

An authenticated non-administrative user could access a Kubernetes cluster they are not authorized to access through GPUStack's Kubernetes API proxy.

The `cluster_apiserver_proxy` handler did not perform a resource-level authorization check before forwarding requests to the selected cluster. Requests were forwarded through a worker using its Kubernetes ServiceAccount credentials.

Depending on the permissions granted to that ServiceAccount, an attacker could read sensitive Kubernetes resources, create or modify workloads, or delete resources and disrupt services. Creating attacker-controlled workloads could result in code execution in the target cluster.

Exploitation requires a Kubernetes-provider cluster with a reachable worker. The operations available to the attacker are limited by the worker's ServiceAccount permissions.

### Patches

Fixed in `gpustack` `v2.2.2`.

### Workarounds

Restrict access to the GPUStack instance to trusted administrator accounts until upgrading.

findings.title: compose-lint: A `.compose-lint.yml` symlinked outside the project is read, and a parse error quotes part of the target
findings.summary:
### Impact

compose-lint automatically reads a `.compose-lint.yml` policy file beside the Compose file. It is meant to read nothing outside the project directory, but it follows that file if it is a symlink, wherever it points.

A pull request can commit `.compose-lint.yml` as a symlink to a file on the CI runner. If the target is not valid YAML, the error compose-lint reports quotes part of the line the parser failed on. That quote reaches the job log (standard error), JSON `errors[]`, and the SARIF `toolExecutionNotifications`, which the Action uploads to Code Scanning. The run exits 2.

What can be read is small. The quote is cut to about 30 characters around the error position, and the attacker cannot choose which line of the target the parser fails on. For an INI-style credentials file, this was the start of the second line (`aws_access_key_id = ` followed by the first characters of the value). Targets in `KEY=value` form, and YAML files that parse, disclosed no values in testing. The pass/fail result is not affected. On a public repository, the job log is visible to the pull request's author.

The Compose file loader stopped quoting source lines in parse errors in 0.25.0 (GHSA-whr6-fgpq-fpv9). The policy loader did not.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**GitHub Action.** Action tags v0.18.0 through v0.31.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless `version:` is set, and so currently install an affected one.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tags 0.3.3 through 0.31.0, the matching minor tags, and `latest` are affected. Inside the container, a symlink resolves within the container, so what can be read is the container's own files and anything mounted into it.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. A `.compose-lint.yml` discovered in the working directory that resolves outside it is refused with exit 2 rather than read, and a policy parse error no longer quotes the line it failed

findings.title: compose-lint: A pull request can make compose-lint quote a secret from a CI-generated `.env` into its findings
findings.summary:
### Impact

Since 0.22.0, compose-lint fills in `${VAR}` references from the `.env` beside the Compose file, as Compose does. The documentation says values under `environment:` are never resolved from a `.env`, "that is where secrets live". But `image:` values are resolved, and CL-0004 and CL-0019 quote the resolved image in their message and fix text.

Some CI workflows write secrets into that `.env` before linting or building. In such a workflow, a pull request that changes one line to `image: "${DB_PASSWORD}"`, or `image: "nginx:${DB_PASSWORD}"`, gets the secret's value quoted in a finding. The finding reaches the job log, JSON output, and the SARIF uploaded to Code Scanning. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text. The pass/fail result is not affected.

This needs a workflow that writes secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file *and* runs on pull requests from authors who should not see them. Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, so the common setup is not exposed, which is why this is scored as low confidentiality impact. Where the conditions hold, such as a `pull_request_target` workflow, pull requests from branches in the same repository, or a self-hosted runner that keeps a populated `.env` in the checkout, the whole value is disclosed.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**GitHub Action.** Action tags v0.22.0 through v0.31.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless `version:` is set, and so currently install an affected one.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tags 0.22.0 through 0.31.0, the matching minor tags, and `latest` are affected when the `.env` is mounted with the project.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. Rules still grade the value the sibling `.env` substituted, but findings, fix guidance and notes quote the `${NAME}` reference in its place, in text, JSON a

findings.title: compose-lint: `fix --apply` can delete a line the user did not select, including a security setting
findings.summary:
### Impact

`compose-lint fix --apply` converts the line numbers its fixers work with into positions in the file. The YAML parser treats a lone carriage return, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 as line breaks, but the conversion counted only `\n`. One of those characters inside a quoted value, which most editors and diff views don't show, shifted every later edit down by one line.

A Compose file from a pull request can use this to make a fix delete the line after the one it meant to change. For example, fixing CL-0014 (`logging: driver: none`) instead removes `driver: none` and the following `networks: [internal]`, moving the service off an internal-only network onto the default bridge. The result is still valid Compose, every check `fix` runs after editing passes, and the command reports `applied 1 fix(es)` and exits 0. A later `compose-lint check` passes too, because no rule requires `networks:`. The dry-run diff (without `--apply`) does show the removed lines, but `--apply` prints only the note for the fix that was selected.

A related crash on the same files could empty the SARIF output for every file in the run. GitHub Code Scanning rejects an empty SARIF upload, which fails the step, so that part does not report a false clean result there.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tags 0.9.0 through 0.17.0, and the matching minor tags, are affected when used to run `fix --apply`. Fixed from `0.18.0`.

The GitHub Action does not run `fix` and is not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.18.0. Line splitting and position conversion now share one definition of a line break, so they can't disagree. A Compose file containing an ambiguous line break (a lone `\r`, U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029) is refused with exit code 2, because no line numbering is correct for both the parser and the editor. CRLF and LF files are unaffected.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.18.0 or later.
- On older versions, review the dry-run diff before

findings.title: compose-lint: Compose file text can issue GitHub Actions workflow commands through the compose-lint Action
findings.summary:
### Impact

The GitHub Actions runner treats certain text in a step's output as commands. The legacy form, `##[command]`, is recognized anywhere in a line. compose-lint's text report prints service names, environment keys and lines of the Compose file, and it does not neutralize `##[`. Inside the compose-lint Action, a Compose file from a pull request can therefore:

- create fake error or warning annotations on the pull request (`##[error]`, `##[warning]`)
- fold the rest of the log, including the real verdict, out of sight (`##[group]`)
- blank out chosen strings for the rest of the log (`##[add-mask]`)

GitHub has postponed removing the deprecated `set-output` log command, so the runner still honors it. A test run of the Action on a GitHub-hosted runner confirmed that a `::set-output` line from a Compose file is processed. Whether it can override the Action's own `sarif-written` output, which decides whether the SARIF upload step runs, has not been tested.

The exit code and the pass/fail result are not affected. Azure Pipelines parses the same `##[` syntax, so the pip package is listed for anyone printing the text report in other CI systems.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.31.0. The Action stops the runner from processing workflow commands while compose-lint's output is printed, using a random `stop-commands` token. The text report also escapes `##[`, and `::` at the start of a line, in anything taken from the Compose file.

### Workarounds

- In your own workflow, wrap the compose-lint step in `::stop-commands::<random token>` and `::<random token>::`.
- Use `--format json` or `--format sarif` rather than the text report when linting untrusted pull requests.

### Reproduction

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: "nginx:1.25"
    environment:
      "##[error]DB_PASSWORD": placeholder
  "##[group]svc":
    image: "nginx:1.25"
    privileged: true
```

Run through the Action, this produces a fake error annotation and fol

findings.title: compose-lint: .env read through a symlink outside the project can expose the CI job's environment
findings.summary:
### Impact

compose-lint fills in `${VAR}` references from the `.env` file next to the Compose file. It is meant to read nothing outside the project directory, and `env_file:`, `include:` and `extends:` paths are checked for that. The `.env` read is not. If `.env` is a symlink, compose-lint follows it wherever it points.

A pull request can add a `.env` symlink to any file on the CI runner and a Compose file that references a variable from it. compose-lint substitutes the value and quotes it in finding messages, which go to the log and to JSON and SARIF output.

The worst target is `/proc/self/environ`, the linter's own environment. The Compose file only needs to reference the name of the first variable in it: because that file separates variables with NUL bytes rather than newlines, the substituted value is the entire rest of the environment. On a CI runner that environment holds whatever the workflow put there, including secrets. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text.

An `include:` entry's `project_directory:` has the same gap from 0.28.0: a directory symlink named there makes compose-lint read `.env` from wherever the link points.

Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, and GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, so in the common setup what can be read is runner metadata and whatever unmasked values the job's environment holds. That is why this is scored as low confidentiality impact. The impact is high in a job that runs untrusted pull requests with secrets in its environment, such as a `pull_request_target` workflow, or on a CI system that does not mask secrets, and also wherever the JSON or SARIF output is uploaded. The pass/fail result is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.31.0. Every `.env` read now applies the same containment check as `env_file:`. A `.env` that resolves outside the project is t

findings.title: Dagu MCP DAG specification read bypasses path containment and workspace isolation
findings.summary:
## Summary

The traversal fix for CVE-2026-33344 was implemented as HTTP middleware installed only in the chi handler chain, but the MCP service calls the same API method in process, so arbitrary YAML file read is reachable again through the MCP tool surface with a viewer-role key. Read-only, limited to .yaml/.yml targets. Confirmed at HEAD f6c039f (post v2.10.7).

## The defect

The fix for CVE-2026-33344 is a reflection-based HTTP middleware (internal/frontend/.../api.go, roughly lines 553-597) that inspects a request field named FileName and rejects anything that is not a plain name. It is installed in exactly one place: the chi strict-handler chain (api.go around line 419).

The MCP service does not go through that chain. internal/service/mcp/server.go calls the API method directly as an in-process Go call:

```go
func (svc *Service) getDAGSpec(ctx context.Context, name string) (map[string]any, error) {   // line 307
    resp, err := svc.api.GetDAGSpec(ctx, daguapi.GetDAGSpecRequestObject{
        FileName: daguapi.DAGFileName(name),                                                 // line 309
    })
```

No HTTP request is constructed, so no middleware executes, and the underlying resolver is still uncontained:

```go
func (store *Storage) locateDAG(nameOrPath string) (string, error) {                 // line 1041
    if strings.Contains(nameOrPath, string(filepath.Separator)) {                    // line 1042
        foundPath, err := findDAGFile(nameOrPath)
        if err == nil {
            return foundPath, nil                                                    // line 1045, no containment check
        }
    }
```

An absolute path contains a separator, so it takes the first branch and is returned as-is, with no check that it falls under store.baseDir or any entry in store.searchPaths.

## Verification

Verified end to end using the project's own conformance/mcptest harness against a real running HTTP server, not by source reading:

```

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ).
